stem: A fresher interview opens with "What is React?" Which two statements belong in a good answer? (Choose two.)

options.text: React is a library for building user interfaces from components; routing, data fetching and forms come from other libraries or from a framework such as Next.js.
options.why: That is React's scope: rendering components and keeping them in sync with state. The rest of the stack is chosen separately.

options.text: React is a full MVC framework that ships with a router, an HTTP client and form validation.
options.why: React has no built-in router or HTTP client. That gap is why React Router, TanStack Query and frameworks like Next.js exist.

options.text: It is declarative: you describe what the UI should look like for the current state, and React works out which DOM changes are needed.
options.why: This is the core idea. You change state and React updates the DOM, instead of you writing each DOM step by hand.

options.text: Data flows both ways: when a child edits a prop, the parent's state updates automatically.
options.why: React uses one-way data flow. Props are read-only, and a child asks the parent for a change by calling a callback the parent passed down.

options.text: Components must be written in JSX, so React cannot run without a JSX compiler.
options.why: JSX is optional syntax that compiles to `jsx()` / `createElement` calls, and you can call those functions directly.

explanation: A strong answer covers three points. React is a UI library, not a whole framework. It is component-based and declarative. Data flows one way, from parent to child. The interviewer is also checking that you know what React does *not* give you, which is why routers, data-fetching libraries and frameworks such as Next.js are built on top of it.

stem: A team starts a plain React app with just `react` and `react-dom` and no framework. Which of these needs does React itself cover, with no extra library?

options.text: Mapping URLs like `/orders/42` to pages, with working Back and Forward buttons
options.why: Client-side routing is not part of React. You add React Router or TanStack Router, or use a framework with file-based routing.

options.text: Giving deeply nested components the signed-in user without prop drilling
options.why: Context (`createContext` with `useContext`, or `use(Context)` in React 19) is built into React for exactly this.

options.text: Caching API responses and refetching them automatically when the browser tab regains focus
options.why: React has no server-data cache. TanStack Query, SWR or a framework's data layer provides that.

options.text: Rendering pages on the server with file-based routes and a separate code-split bundle per page
options.why: React has low-level server-rendering APIs, but file-based routing and per-route bundles come from a framework such as Next.js.

explanation: React covers components, state, effects, context and rendering to the DOM, plus low-level server-rendering APIs. Routing, server-state caching and build concerns such as file-based routes come from libraries or frameworks. When interviewers ask "library or framework?", they want to see that you know where React's job ends.
reference: react.dev: Passing Data Deeply with Context

stem: Your team writes only function components with hooks. Which piece still has to be a class component in React 19?

options.text: A component that must reset its state when its `userId` prop changes
options.why: Give it `key={userId}` from the parent so React remounts it with fresh state. No class is needed.

options.text: An error boundary that shows a fallback UI when a child throws while rendering
options.why: Catching render errors needs `static getDerivedStateFromError` or `componentDidCatch`, and no hook does this yet. Libraries such as react-error-boundary wrap a class for you.

options.text: A component that subscribes to a browser API and must unsubscribe when it unmounts
options.why: `useEffect` with a cleanup function, or `useSyncExternalStore`, covers subscriptions.

options.text: A component that measures a DOM node's size right after it renders, before the browser paints
options.why: `useRef` plus `useLayoutEffect` reads layout after the DOM update and before paint.

explanation: Hooks replaced almost everything classes were used for: state with `useState`, lifecycle with `useEffect`, instance fields with `useRef`, and shared logic with custom hooks instead of HOCs. The one gap is error boundaries. React only calls `getDerivedStateFromError` and `componentDidCatch` on class components, so you write one small class (or use a library) and wrap your function components in it.
reference: react.dev: Component (Catching rendering errors with an error boundary)

options.text: It throws a TypeError, because `this` is `undefined` inside `handleClick`
options.why: The method is passed as a bare function and class bodies run in strict mode, so `this` is lost when React calls it. An arrow field or `.bind(this)` fixes the binding.

options.text: It works and shows "On", because React binds component methods to the instance automatically
options.why: The old `createReactClass` API did autobind, but ES6 classes do not. React calls the handler without an instance.

options.text: Nothing happens; the prop should be `onClick={this.handleClick()}` so that the method actually runs
options.why: That calls `handleClick` during every render and passes its return value (`undefined`) as the handler. Calling setState while rendering is also an error.

options.text: It throws, because a class component cannot declare `state` as a class field outside the constructor
options.why: Class fields are standard JavaScript, and `state = {...}` is a common way to initialise state in a class component.

explanation: Class methods are not bound to the instance. `onClick={this.handleClick}` passes the plain function, and because class bodies are strict-mode code, `this` is `undefined` when it is called. The usual fixes are `handleClick = () => {...}` or `this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this)` in the constructor. Function components avoid this whole category of bug. When interviewers compare the two styles, this is the point they want you to raise, along with hooks replacing lifecycle methods.

stem: An `<Accordion multiple={bool}>` must allow only one open section when `multiple` is false and any number when it is true. Clicking an open section closes it. State is `const [openIds, setOpenIds] = useState(() => new Set());`. Which toggle meets every requirement?

options.text: `setOpenIds(prev => { prev.has(id) ? prev.delete(id) : prev.add(id); return prev; })`
options.why: It mutates the existing Set and returns the same object. React compares with `Object.is`, sees no change and skips the re-render.

options.text: `setOpenIds(prev => new Set(multiple ? [...prev, id] : [id]))`
options.why: An open section can never close: adding an id that is already in a Set does nothing, so clicking it again keeps it open.

options.text: `setOpenIds(prev => { const next = new Set(multiple ? prev : []); prev.has(id) ? next.delete(id) : next.add(id); return next; })`
options.why: It always returns a new Set. In single mode it starts empty, so opening one section closes the others, and clicking the open one leaves it closed.

options.text: `setOpenIds(prev => { const next = new Set(prev); if (!multiple) next.clear(); next.has(id) ? next.delete(id) : next.add(id); return next; })`
options.why: In single mode it clears the Set before checking, so clicking the open section adds it straight back and it never closes.

explanation: A Set of open ids covers both modes: single mode is the same structure with at most one entry. The two classic mistakes are mutating the Set (React bails out because the reference did not change) and forgetting the close path. Always build a new Set or array when updating state that holds a collection.

options.text: The Shipping body appears under the first header
options.why: `openIndex && ...` short-circuits on 0, so the paragraph is never created for index 0.

options.text: Neither body appears, and a stray "0" is shown under both headers
options.why: In every section `openIndex && ...` evaluates to the number 0, and React renders numbers as text.

options.text: A stray "0" appears under the Shipping header only, and Returns renders normally
options.why: The same expression runs in each section, and each one evaluates to 0, so both sections render it.

options.text: Nothing changes, because React ignores `setOpenIndex(0)` when the new value is falsy
options.why: React stores 0 like any other value, and the state does change. The bug is in the render expression.

explanation:
Index 0 is a valid index and also falsy. `a && b` returns `a` when it is falsy, so every section renders the number 0 and no body appears. Write `openIndex === i &&

…

`; the strict comparison alone is enough. The other sections (index 1 and above) work, which is why this bug often survives a quick manual test.

stem: You are asked to make the accordion work for keyboard and screen-reader users. Which two changes match the WAI-ARIA accordion pattern? (Choose two.)

options.text: Make each header a `<button>` (inside a heading element) so it can be focused and toggled with Enter or Space
options.why: A real button is focusable and handles Enter and Space natively; the heading keeps the page outline meaningful.

options.text: Set `aria-expanded` on each header button to match whether its panel is open, and point `aria-controls` at the panel's `id`
options.why: This is how assistive technology announces "expanded" or "collapsed" and links the header to its content.

options.text: Put `onClick` on a `<div>` header and add a `title` attribute describing the section
options.why: A div is not focusable and does not respond to Enter or Space, so keyboard users cannot open it.

options.text: Mark the open header with `aria-selected="true"` and wrap all headers in `role="tablist"`
options.why: Those roles belong to the tabs pattern. An accordion uses `aria-expanded` on buttons.

options.text: Give every panel `tabIndex={0}` so users can Tab through closed panels' content too
options.why: Closed panels should be hidden from everyone. Making hidden content focusable creates invisible tab stops.

explanation: The WAI-ARIA accordion pattern is a heading containing a button for each section. The button carries `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, and the panel has the matching `id` (optionally `role="region"` with `aria-labelledby`). Interviewers at product companies often ask for accessibility after the basic build works, so name these attributes without being prompted.

stem: A `<StarRating>` will be used in a review form that resets after submit, and as a read-only display on product cards. Which component API fits?

options.text: `<StarRating initialRating={3} />`, which keeps the rating in its own state and exposes nothing else
options.why: The form can never read the chosen value or reset it, because the state is private to the widget.

options.text: A controlled API: `value` and `onChange(n)` props with the parent owning the rating, plus a `readOnly` flag
options.why: The parent can read, validate and reset the value, exactly like a controlled `<input>`, and `readOnly` covers the display case.

options.text: Internal state that a useEffect copies from a `rating` prop, with the form reading the current value through a ref
options.why: This creates two sources of truth that drift apart, and reading values through refs skips React's data flow.

options.text: The widget writes the rating to `localStorage` and the form reads it back when the user submits
options.why: Global storage is shared by every instance, does not re-render the parent, and leaks between forms.

explanation: A reusable form control should behave like the built-in ones: controlled through `value` and `onChange`, optionally uncontrolled through `defaultValue`. The parent then owns the data and can validate, submit and reset it. Interviewers use this question to see whether you design the API before writing the stars.
reference: react.dev: Sharing State Between Components (controlled and uncontrolled components)

options.text: Three filled stars: `hover` is 0, which is falsy, so `shown` falls back to `value`
options.why: That is how `||` behaves. `??` falls back only for `null` and `undefined`, and 0 is neither.

options.text: Five empty stars: `??` keeps the 0 set on mouse leave, so `shown` is 0
options.why: 0 is not nullish, so `hover ?? value` is 0 and no star satisfies `n <= 0`.

options.text: The last hovered count stays filled, because `onMouseLeave` does not fire on a wrapper `<div>`
options.why: `onMouseLeave` fires when the pointer leaves that element, wrapper or not. The handler runs and sets 0.

options.text: Three filled stars, but only after a short delay, because hover updates are deferred
options.why: State updates from pointer events are not deferred. The next render shows the 0 immediately.

explanation: The hover preview should be derived as `hover ?? value`, with "no hover" represented by `null`. Resetting to `null` on mouse leave fixes the bug. Switching to `||` also hides it, but then a legitimate 0 can never be shown. The interviewer is checking that you know the difference between nullish and falsy, and that you derive the shown value instead of storing a third piece of state.

stem: An interviewer asks how keyboard and screen-reader users will use your star rating. Which two approaches work? (Choose two.)

options.text: Render the stars as radio inputs that share one `name`, each labelled like "4 stars", so arrow keys change the choice and the value is submitted with the form
options.why: Native radios give keyboard support, a checked state that is announced, and form submission without extra code.

options.text: Group the stars in a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`, or a `role="radiogroup"` with an accessible name, so the question is announced
options.why: Screen readers then announce something like "Rating, 4 stars, 3 of 5" instead of a list of unlabelled controls.

options.text: Use `<span>` stars with `onClick` and a `title` tooltip on each
options.why: Spans are not focusable and ignore Enter and Space, and `title` is not a reliable accessible name.

options.text: Mark the selected star with `aria-pressed="true"` on a `<div>` and leave the other stars unmarked
options.why: A div still is not focusable, and toggle-button semantics do not describe choosing one value out of five.

options.text: Show the rating only through filled and empty colours, and rely on hover to preview a choice
options.why: Colour alone fails users who cannot see it, and hover does not exist for keyboard or touch users.

explanation: A star rating is a single choice from a set, which is exactly what a radio group expresses. Visually hidden radio inputs with labels, styled as stars, give focus, arrow-key navigation, announcements and form participation for free. Interviewers ask about this to see whether you reach for native semantics before custom ARIA.

options.text: `object h1 { className: 'title', children: 'Hi' }`
options.why: JSX creates a React element: a plain object with `type`, `props` and `key`. The text becomes `props.children`.

options.text: `object HTMLHeadingElement { className: 'title' }`
options.why: No DOM node exists yet. JSX only describes the UI; React creates DOM nodes later, during commit.

options.text: `string h1 { class: 'title', children: 'Hi' }`
options.why: JSX does not produce HTML strings, and the prop keeps its JSX name `className`.

options.text: `object FiberNode { className: 'title', children: 'Hi' }`
options.why: Fibers are React's internal work units, created while rendering. JSX itself only returns a lightweight element.

explanation: A React element is a small, immutable, plain object describing what to show. The tree of these elements that your components return is what people call the "virtual DOM". It is cheap to create, and React compares it with the previous tree to decide which real DOM changes to make. Interviewers ask this to check that you know the virtual DOM is just data, not a second browser DOM.
reference: react.dev: Writing Markup with JSX; react.dev: createElement

stem: Which two statements about React's virtual DOM are accurate? (Choose two.)

options.text: It makes React faster than carefully hand-written DOM updates, because the virtual DOM is a faster copy of the browser DOM
options.why: Diffing is extra work on top of the DOM writes. Its value is that declarative code is fast enough by default, not that it beats optimal manual updates.

options.text: It is a tree of plain JavaScript objects describing the UI; React compares the new tree with the previous one to find what changed
options.why: Components return element trees, and reconciliation diffs them to work out the minimum set of DOM operations.

options.text: It is a browser feature, like the Shadow DOM, that React switches on for each component
options.why: The virtual DOM lives entirely in React's JavaScript. Shadow DOM is a separate browser feature for encapsulating web components.

options.text: The comparison happens in memory during the render phase; real DOM nodes are only created or changed in the commit phase
options.why: Rendering calls components and diffs the results; committing applies the resulting changes to the DOM.

options.text: On each state change React rebuilds the real DOM, then patches the differences back into the virtual DOM
options.why: It is the other way round: React re-renders the virtual tree and writes only the differences to the real DOM.

explanation: The honest interview answer: the virtual DOM is an in-memory description of the UI. React re-renders it on state changes, diffs it against the previous one, and commits only the differences to the real DOM. It is not inherently faster than optimal direct DOM code. Frameworks such as Svelte and Solid skip it entirely. What it buys you is declarative code with good-enough performance by default.
reference: react.dev: Render and Commit; react.dev: Preserving and Resetting State

options.text: React replaces the `<div>` and its children with freshly created nodes
options.why: React recreates nodes only when an element's type or key changes at that position. Here nothing changed.

options.text: React skips calling `StoreHours`, because it can tell the JSX would be the same
options.why: The state changed, so React must call the component to find out what it returns. It cannot know the output in advance.

options.text: The component runs, the new tree matches the previous one, and the commit makes no DOM changes
options.why: Rendering produces a new element tree; diffing finds no differences, so there is nothing to write to the DOM.

options.text: React sets the `innerHTML` of the `<div>` to the same markup, which the browser treats as a no-op
options.why: React never uses `innerHTML` for normal updates. It changes individual nodes, attributes and text.

explanation: Re-rendering means calling your component; it does not mean touching the DOM. React only changes DOM nodes that differ between renders, so an identical tree costs a function call and a diff but no DOM writes. Interviewers use this to separate "render" from "commit", and to show why an unnecessary re-render is usually cheap.

stem: Which two statements about props and state are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Props are inputs owned by the parent; the child reads them but must not change them
options.why: Props describe how the parent configured the child, and they are read-only from the child's point of view.

options.text: A child can update a prop by assigning `props.title = 'x'`, and the parent re-renders with the new value
options.why: Mutating props never reaches the parent. In development React freezes the props object, so the assignment throws in strict-mode code.

options.text: State belongs to the component that declares it and survives re-renders; calling its setter re-renders that component and its children
options.why: State is the component's own memory, kept by React between renders and changed only through the setter.

options.text: Every instance of a component shares the same state, so two `<Counter />` elements always show the same number
options.why: Each rendered instance has its own state. Two counters count independently.

options.text: When the parent passes a new prop value, `useState(prop)` in the child resets to that value automatically
options.why: The argument to `useState` is only the initial value. Later prop changes are ignored unless you handle them yourself.

explanation: Props flow down from the parent and are read-only; state is private to the component and changes through its setter, which triggers a re-render. A good answer adds that a child changes data it does not own by calling a callback prop, and that copying a prop into state only uses the first value.
reference: react.dev: Passing Props to a Component; react.dev: State: A Component's Memory

stem: `<ProductSearch products={products} />` receives the product list from its parent. It has a search box and shows only the products whose name contains the typed text. What should be state inside `ProductSearch`?

options.text: The search text and the filtered list, kept in sync with a useEffect that runs when either changes
options.why: The filtered list is redundant. Syncing it in an effect adds an extra render and briefly shows a stale list.

options.text: A copy of `products`, so the component can filter that copy in place as the user types
options.why: Copying a prop into state stops following the parent's updates, and filtering in place loses products for good.

options.text: Only the search text; the filtered list is computed from `products` and the text during render
options.why: `products` is a prop and the filtered list can be derived, so the typed text is the only thing that needs state.

options.text: Nothing: read the input's current value through a ref during each render
options.why: Typing does not change any state, so the component never re-renders to show new results.

explanation: Keep state minimal. Ask of every value: is it passed in as a prop? Can it be computed from props and other state? If either answer is yes, it is not state. Here only the query is state, and `products.filter(...)` runs during render (use `useMemo` if it is measurably slow).
reference: react.dev: Thinking in React (Find the minimal but complete representation of UI state)

stem: A `<ColorPicker>` child must tell its parent `<Editor>` which colour the user clicked, so the parent can store it in its own state. Which approach follows React's data flow?

options.text: The child assigns `props.color = c`, and the parent reads `color` on its next render
options.why: Props are read-only and belong to the parent. Assigning to them changes nothing the parent can see.

options.text: The child dispatches a `CustomEvent` on `window`, and the parent listens for it in a useEffect
options.why: It can be made to work, but it bypasses props, is global, and is hard to trace. It is not how React components talk.

options.text: The parent reads the child's internal state through a ref after every click
options.why: A ref to a function component does not expose its state, and reading a ref does not trigger a re-render.

options.text: The parent passes `onPick={setColor}`, and the child calls `onPick(c)` in its click handler
options.why: Data goes down as props and events come up as callback calls. The parent's setter updates its state and React re-renders.

explanation: In React, data flows one way: parents pass values and callbacks down, and children report events by calling those callbacks. The parent stays the single owner of the value. This is the answer interviewers expect for "how does a child send data to its parent?"

stem: `<Filters>` and `<ResultsList>` are siblings under `<SearchPage>`. When the user picks a category in `Filters`, the list must update. Which design should you pick?

options.text: Lift `category` into `SearchPage` and pass it down, plus a setter callback for `Filters`
options.why: The closest common parent owns the value, so both siblings render from one source of truth.

options.text: Each sibling keeps its own `category` state, and `Filters` copies its value into `ResultsList` with a useEffect
options.why: A component cannot set a sibling's state. There is no way for `Filters` to reach into `ResultsList`.

options.text: Store the category in a module-level variable that both components import and read
options.why: Changing a plain variable does not trigger a re-render, so `ResultsList` keeps showing old results.

options.text: Have `ResultsList` read the selected `<option>` from the DOM with `document.querySelector` while it renders
options.why: Nothing re-renders `ResultsList` when the selection changes, and reading the DOM during render is unreliable.

explanation: When two components need the same changing data, move the state up to their closest common parent and pass it down. This "lifting state up" is the usual answer before reaching for Context or a store, which help only when the common parent is far away.

options.text: Effects may not call `fetch`; data loading must happen in an event handler instead
options.why: Fetching in an effect is allowed. The problem is only how the effect function is declared.

options.text: The async callback returns a Promise where React expects a cleanup function or nothing
options.why: React treats the return value as cleanup. Declare an async function inside the effect and call it, which also leaves room for a real cleanup.

options.text: Nothing: React awaits the returned promise before it commits the render
options.why: React never awaits effects. They run after commit and their return value is stored as the cleanup.

options.text: It must be a `useLayoutEffect`, because only layout effects can be async functions
options.why: Neither hook accepts an async function. `useLayoutEffect` only changes when the effect runs.

explanation: An effect must return nothing or a cleanup function. An async function always returns a Promise, so React 19 logs "useEffect must not return anything besides a function" and suggests the fix. Write `useEffect(() => { async function load() {…} load(); return () => {…}; }, [id])`. The cleanup slot is where you add an `ignore` flag or `AbortController` so a slow response for an old `id` cannot overwrite the new one.

options.text: Call `setLoading(false)` before `await getOrders()`
options.why: Then the spinner is cleared before the request finishes, so it is never visible while loading.

options.text: Derive loading as `!orders && !error` and delete the `loading` state
options.why: This breaks on reload: once orders exist, a refetch never shows a spinner.

options.text: Move `setLoading(false)` out of the `try` and into a `finally` block
options.why: `finally` runs after success and after failure, so the spinner always stops.

options.text: Wrap `setLoading(true)` in `startTransition` so React can drop it when the request fails
options.why: Transitions change update priority. They do not undo a state update when a promise rejects.

explanation: The happy path cleared the flag; the error path forgot to. Clearing it in `finally` covers both. Many teams go further and keep a single `status` (`'idle' | 'loading' | 'error' | 'success'`), which makes impossible combinations such as "loading and error at once" unrepresentable.

options.text: The error message, because `fetch` rejects when the status is 404
options.why: `fetch` resolves for any HTTP response, including 4xx and 5xx. It rejects only on network failure or abort.

options.text: The error message, because `res.json()` throws when it is called on an error response
options.why: The body is valid JSON, so `res.json()` parses it normally. The status code does not affect parsing.

options.text: No error: `user` becomes `{ message: 'User not found' }`
options.why: The 404 resolves, the body parses, and the error object is stored as if it were a user. Check `res.ok` and throw to reach the `catch`.

options.text: Nothing, because the 404 sets the `ignore` flag and both state updates are skipped
options.why: `ignore` is set only by the cleanup when `id` changes or the component unmounts, not by the response status.

explanation: `fetch` treats any HTTP response as success. Add `if (!res.ok) throw new Error(...)` before parsing, or use a client such as axios, which rejects on non-2xx statuses by default. Interviewers like this because the code looks complete (it has try/catch and a race guard) but still shows a broken UI for a common error.
reference: MDN: Using the Fetch API (Checking that the fetch was successful)

options.text: The row is styled as done and the count drops, because `map` returns a new array
options.why: The new array re-renders `TodoList`, but `memo` compares each `todo` prop by reference, and the mutated object is the same reference.

options.text: The "left" count drops by one, but the clicked row keeps its old style
options.why: The parent re-renders and counts the mutated `done` flag, while the memoised row sees identical props and is skipped.

options.text: Nothing changes, because React cannot detect mutations at all
options.why: The updater returns a new array, so React does see a change and re-renders `TodoList`.

options.text: The row is styled as done, but the count stays the same
options.why: It is the other way round. The parent that computes the count re-renders; the memoised row does not.

explanation: Updating `todos` immutably means a new array *and* a new object for the changed todo: `prev.map(t => t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)`. Mutating the object keeps its reference, so anything that compares by reference (`memo`, `useMemo` dependencies, selectors) misses the change. StrictMode calls updater functions twice in development precisely to expose impure updaters like this one. In a todo machine-coding round, interviewers watch for this toggle.
reference: react.dev: Updating Arrays in State; react.dev: memo

options.text: Spreading `prev` copies the old ids onto the new todos; building the array with `concat` avoids it
options.why: Spreading copies the old items unchanged and does not touch the new ones. `concat` would behave the same way.

options.text: All three got the same `Date.now()` id; use `crypto.randomUUID()` instead
options.why: The `map` runs within one millisecond, and `Date.now()` has millisecond resolution, so all three ids are equal. React also warns about duplicate keys.

options.text: Todos that are added together must use the array index as their `key`
options.why: The key is not the problem; the delete filter matches by id. Index keys would cause other bugs when rows are removed.

options.text: The delete handler reads a stale `todos` array; switching it to an updater function fixes it
options.why: Even with fresh state, filtering out one shared id still removes all three todos.

explanation: `Date.now()` is not an id generator. Several items created in the same tick (or by two fast clicks) collide, which breaks keys, toggles and deletes together. Use `crypto.randomUUID()` or an incrementing counter, or take the id from the server. Duplicate keys also make React warn and may reuse the wrong row's DOM.
reference: react.dev: Rendering Lists (Where to get your key); MDN: Crypto.randomUUID()

options.text: Also call `setVisible` in `addTodo`, and in every other handler that changes `todos`
options.why: This patches the symptom, but every future handler (toggle, edit, delete) must remember to resync, and the two copies will drift again.

options.text: Add a useEffect that calls `setVisible` whenever `todos` or `filter` change
options.why: It works, but each change first renders the stale list, then renders again after the effect. It is redundant state.

options.text: Keep `visible` in a `useRef` instead, so it always holds the latest list
options.why: Updating a ref does not re-render, so the list on screen still does not change.

options.text: Remove the `visible` state and derive the list during render
options.why: The visible list is fully determined by the other two values, so deriving it can never go out of sync.

explanation: If a value can be computed from props and state, compute it during render instead of storing it. Here `const visible = todos.filter(...)` replaces a state variable and the code that kept it in sync. Wrap it in `useMemo` only if profiling shows the filter is expensive. Interviewers ask this as a follow-up to the todo build to check that you avoid duplicated state.
reference: react.dev: You Might Not Need an Effect (Updating state based on props or state)

stem: Requirements: three buttons that each show their own click count, a "Total" line with the sum, a "Reset all" button, and adding a fourth button should take one change. Which state design meets every requirement?

options.text: Each `<CounterButton>` keeps its own `useState(0)` and calls an `onClick` prop, so the parent can increment a separate `total` state
options.why: "Reset all" cannot reach the private count inside each button, and `total` is a second copy of data that can drift.

options.text: One `counts` array in the parent, passed down with `onIncrement(i)`; the total is summed during render
options.why: One source of truth: reset replaces the array, a new button is one more array entry, and the total cannot disagree with the counts.

options.text: Separate `count1`, `count2`, `count3` and `total` state in the parent, with each click handler also incrementing `total`
options.why: Every new button needs new state and a new handler, and `total` duplicates information already in the counts.

options.text: A module-level `counts` array that each button mutates, with the total read from it during render
options.why: Mutating a plain module variable never triggers a re-render, and every mounted instance would share it.

explanation: Put the state in the closest common owner, use a collection when the number of items can grow, and derive totals instead of storing them. Flipkart and Uber have used this exercise to check exactly those three habits before moving on to harder follow-ups.
reference: react.dev: Sharing State Between Components; react.dev: Choosing the State Structure

options.text: Buttons 2, 0, 0 and "Total: 2"
options.why: That needs `reduce` to see the updated counts, but `counts` is still the snapshot from the render the click happened in.

options.text: Buttons 2, 0, 0 and "Total: 0"
options.why: The second click sums the snapshot `[1, 0, 0]`, so the total does move to 1.

options.text: Buttons 1, 0, 0 and "Total: 1"
options.why: Each click maps over the latest rendered counts, so the first button does reach 2.

options.text: Buttons 2, 0, 0 and "Total: 1"
options.why: The total is computed from the counts before each click: 0 after the first click, 1 after the second. It always lags one click behind.

explanation: `setCounts` does not change `counts` in the running handler. State is a snapshot, so `reduce` sums the old array. Storing a total that can be computed is the root cause: delete `total` and render `counts.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)`.
reference: react.dev: State as a Snapshot; react.dev: Choosing the State Structure (Avoid redundant state)

stem: Which two pieces of markup does the WAI-ARIA tabs pattern expect? (Choose two.)

options.text: Tabs use `role="menuitem"` inside a `role="menu"`, since clicking one changes what is shown
options.why: Menus are for lists of actions or commands. Switching between views of content is the tabs pattern.

options.text: A `role="tablist"` container holding buttons with `role="tab"`, where only the active tab has `aria-selected="true"`
options.why: This is how screen readers announce "tab, 2 of 3, selected".

options.text: Each tab carries `aria-expanded` that toggles like an accordion header
options.why: `aria-expanded` belongs to disclosure and accordion buttons. Tabs use `aria-selected`.

options.text: Each panel has `role="tabpanel"` and `aria-labelledby` pointing at its tab, and each tab's `aria-controls` points at its panel
options.why: These links tie each panel to the tab that names it, in both directions.

options.text: Every tab stays in the Tab order with `tabIndex={0}`, so users press Tab to move between tabs
options.why: The pattern uses a roving tabindex: only the active tab is tabbable, and arrow keys move between tabs.

explanation: A tabs widget needs `tablist`, `tab` (with `aria-selected` and `aria-controls`) and `tabpanel` (with `aria-labelledby`), plus keyboard support: arrow keys move between tabs, and only the active tab is in the Tab order. Interviewers who ask for an "accessible tabs component" expect you to name these without looking them up.

stem: The active tab must survive a page refresh, be shareable as `/settings?tab=billing`, and follow the browser's Back button. Using React Router, which approach meets all three?

options.text: `useState(searchParams.get('tab') ?? 'profile')`, plus a useEffect that writes the tab to the URL when it changes
options.why: The URL is read only once, as the initial value. When Back changes the URL, the state does not follow.

options.text: Read the tab from `useSearchParams()` on every render and change it with `setSearchParams`
options.why: With `searchParams.get('tab') ?? 'profile'` and `setSearchParams({ tab: id })`, the URL is the single source of truth. Router navigation, including Back and Forward, re-renders the component with the new value.

options.text: Store the active tab in `localStorage` and read it when the component mounts
options.why: It survives a refresh, but the link cannot be shared and Back does not change the tab.

options.text: Read `window.location.search` during render and call `history.pushState` on click
options.why: `pushState` does not notify React or the router, so nothing re-renders when a tab is clicked.

explanation: When state must live in the URL, make the URL the only copy: read the search param during render and update it through the router. Mirroring it into `useState` creates two sources of truth, and they get out of sync on Back and Forward. `setSearchParams` pushes a history entry by default; pass `{ replace: true }` if tab changes should not fill the history.

stem: With `<Route path="/users/:userId" element={<UserPage />} />`, which line inside `UserPage` reads `42` from `/users/42` in React Router v6 or v7?

options.text: `const { userId } = props.match.params;`
options.why: That was the React Router v5 API. In v6 and later, route elements receive no `match` prop.

options.text: `const userId = useSearchParams()[0].get('userId');`
options.why: Search params read the query string (`?userId=42`), not a path segment.

options.text: `const { userId } = useParams();`
options.why: `useParams` returns the dynamic segments of the matched route. Note that the value is the string `"42"`.

options.text: `const { userId } = useLocation().params;`
options.why: The location object has `pathname`, `search`, `hash` and `state`, but no `params`.

explanation: Dynamic segments such as `:userId` come from `useParams()`, always as strings, so convert them before comparing with numeric ids. Query strings come from `useSearchParams()`. Interviews for junior roles often check that you know the v6+ hooks instead of the v5 `match` prop.

stem: In a React Router v6 or v7 app, which two snippets are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: `<Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />` inside `<Routes>`, to show a 404 page for any URL no other route matches
options.why: A splat path matches anything, and the router ranks it below every more specific route.

options.text: `<Redirect from="/home" to="/" />`, to send an old URL to the new one
options.why: `<Redirect>` was removed in v6. Use `<Navigate>` in a route element instead.

options.text: `<Route path="/home" element={<Navigate to="/" replace />} />`, to send an old URL to the new one
options.why: `<Navigate>` performs the redirect when rendered, and `replace` keeps the old URL out of the history stack.

options.text: `const history = useHistory();` and then `history.push('/orders')` after the form is saved
options.why: `useHistory` is the v5 API. In v6 and later, use `const navigate = useNavigate()` and call `navigate('/orders')`.

options.text: A route with `path="/404"`, which React Router renders automatically whenever no other route matches
options.why: React Router has no special `/404` path. Unmatched URLs only render something if you declare a `*` route.

explanation: The core React Router v6/v7 vocabulary is `<Routes>` / `<Route>`, `useParams`, `useNavigate` for navigation from handlers, `<Navigate>` for declarative redirects, and a `*` route for 404 pages. Many candidates still answer with v5 APIs (`Switch`, `Redirect`, `useHistory`), and interviewers notice.
reference: React Router: Routing; React Router: Navigate

stem: A `<PageLayout>` must show a different header area and sidebar on each page (a search box on one page, filters on another), with the page content in the middle. Which API is the idiomatic React design?

options.text: `class SearchPage extends PageLayout`, overriding `renderHeader()` and `renderSidebar()`
options.why: React recommends composition over inheritance. Subclassing components couples pages to the layout's internals.

options.text: Boolean props such as `showSearch`, `showFilters` and `showDateRange`, with `PageLayout` importing every possible widget
options.why: The layout grows with every page and depends on all of them. Each new variation means another prop.

options.text: `<PageLayout header={<SearchBox />} sidebar={<Filters />}>{content}</PageLayout>`, rendering each slot in place
options.why: Elements passed as props act like named slots. The layout positions them without knowing what they are.

options.text: Pass everything as `children` and have `PageLayout` pick the header and sidebar by position with `Children.toArray`
options.why: Position-based picking breaks as soon as a page wraps items in a fragment or changes their order.

explanation: JSX elements are values, so you can pass them in any prop, not only `children`. Named "slot" props such as `header` and `sidebar` keep the layout generic and let each page decide what goes in. This also solves many prop-drilling problems: the page renders `<SearchBox query={query} />` itself instead of threading `query` through the layout.
reference: react.dev: Passing Props to a Component (Passing JSX as children)

stem: A dashboard loads three independent widgets (orders, stats and users) in one effect. Requirements: start all three requests at once, and if one API fails, show an error in that widget only while the other two still render. Which approach fits?

options.text: `await Promise.all([...])` in a try/catch, and set a dashboard error in the `catch`
options.why: `Promise.all` rejects as soon as any request fails, so the two successful results are lost.

options.text: Three `await` calls in a row, each wrapped in its own try/catch
options.why: Failures are isolated, but each request waits for the previous one, creating a waterfall instead of starting all three at once.

options.text: `await Promise.allSettled([...])`, then fill each widget from its own result
options.why: All requests run in parallel, and `allSettled` waits for every one, reporting each as `{ status, value }` or `{ status, reason }`.

options.text: `await Promise.race([...])`, and render whichever result arrives first
options.why: `race` settles with the first result only. The other two widgets never get their data.

explanation: Pick the combinator that matches the UI. `Promise.all` is all-or-nothing (fail-fast). `Promise.allSettled` gives partial results. `Promise.race` and `Promise.any` settle on the first result. Letting each widget fetch its own data, in its own component, is another good answer for a dashboard. Either way, start requests together and avoid sequential awaits.

options.text: `failed: stats after ~100ms`
options.why: `Promise.all` rejects with the first rejection, as soon as it happens, without waiting for the rest.

options.text: `failed: stats after ~300ms`
options.why: That would mean waiting for every promise to settle first, which is what `allSettled` does, not `all`.

options.text: `ok [ 'orders', undefined, 'users' ]`
options.why: A rejected input does not become `undefined`; it rejects the whole `Promise.all`.

options.text: `failed: stats after ~600ms`
options.why: The timers run in parallel, not one after another, so no step takes 600 ms.

explanation: `Promise.all` is fail-fast: it rejects as soon as one input rejects, with that reason. The other requests keep running in the background, because promises cannot be cancelled. Use an `AbortController` if you need to stop them. A favourite follow-up is to implement `Promise.all` yourself: resolve when a counter reaches the input length, store results by index, and reject on the first error.

options.text: It wraps to the last slide, index 4
options.why: In JavaScript, `%` keeps the sign of the left operand, so `-1 % 5` is `-1`, not 4.

options.text: `index` stays 0, because `%` never returns a negative number
options.why: JavaScript's `%` is a remainder, not a mathematical modulo, and it can be negative.

options.text: `index` becomes -1, and reading `slides[-1].src` throws a TypeError
options.why: `slides[-1]` is `undefined`. The fix is `(i - 1 + slides.length) % slides.length`, which stays non-negative.

options.text: `index` becomes `NaN`, so the carousel renders an empty image
options.why: `-1 % 5` is the ordinary number -1, not `NaN`.

explanation: Wrap-around in both directions is `(i + 1) % n` for next and `(i - 1 + n) % n` for previous. The bug only shows up on the first slide, so it is easy to miss when testing. It is one of the first things interviewers check in a carousel round.

options.text: Version 1
options.why: It advances and wraps correctly, but the interval ignores manual clicks: a click 2.9 s into the cycle is followed by an automatic move 0.1 s later.

options.text: Version 2
options.why: Every index change, automatic or manual, cleans up the pending timeout and starts a fresh 3-second one, and unmount clears it too.

options.text: Version 3
options.why: Without cleanup, the old timeout still fires after a manual click, so the slide jumps early, and a timer can fire after unmount.

options.text: Version 4
options.why: With empty dependencies, the callback always sees `index` from the first render, so the carousel moves to slide 1 and stays there.

explanation: Putting `index` in the dependencies turns the effect into "wait 3 seconds after the slide last changed". The cleanup cancels the pending timer whenever the slide changes for any reason, and on unmount. Interviewers often add "pause on hover" next; that is one more dependency (`paused`) and an early return in the effect.
reference: react.dev: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects; react.dev: Synchronizing with Effects

options.text: s3, s4 and s0, because `slice` wraps around past the end of the array
options.why: `slice` never wraps. It stops at the end of the array.

options.text: s3, s4 and `undefined`, which crashes when the third image reads `s.id`
options.why: `slice` returns only the items that exist, so there is no `undefined` entry and no crash.

options.text: Only s3 and s4; map each position k to `slides[(index + k) % slides.length]`
options.why: `slice(3, 6)` returns two items. `Array.from({ length: perView }, (_, k) => slides[(index + k) % n])` gives s3, s4 and s0.

options.text: Only s3 and s4; fix it with `slides.slice(index % perView, index % perView + perView)`
options.why: At index 3 this gives `slice(0, 3)`, which shows s0 to s2: the wrong slides.

explanation: With several slides per view, each visible position needs its own wrap: `slides[(index + k) % n]` for k from 0 to `perView - 1`. The alternative is to clamp `index` to `n - perView` and disable Next at the end. Both are fine, as long as you say which behaviour you chose. The keys stay unique as long as `perView` is at most the number of slides.

stem: In a Tic-Tac-Toe component, the board is `useState(Array(9).fill(null))` and `calculateWinner(board)` returns `'X'`, `'O'` or `null`. Where should the winner come from?

options.text: A `winner` state that a useEffect sets whenever `board` changes
options.why: Duplicate state that lags one render behind. Until the effect runs, the board shows three in a row and no winner.

options.text: A `winner` state set in the click handler with `setWinner(calculateWinner(board))` right after `setBoard(next)`
options.why: `board` is still the snapshot from before the move, so the winning move is never detected until the next click.

options.text: `const winner = calculateWinner(board)` during render
options.why: The board fully determines the result, so deriving it is always in sync. A draw is `!winner && board.every(Boolean)`.

options.text: Separate `xMoves` and `oMoves` arrays in state alongside `board`, and compute the winner from those
options.why: Three copies of the same information must be updated together; any slip makes them disagree.

explanation: Store the minimum state, here the board (or the move history), and derive everything else: winner, draw, and whose turn it is (from the number of filled squares). This is exactly what interviewers look for in a Tic-Tac-Toe round. Then they ask about an N x N board and an O(1) win check.
reference: react.dev: Tutorial: Tic-Tac-Toe; react.dev: Choosing the State Structure

options.text: An empty board, because each move copies the board before writing to it
options.why: `[...board]` copies only the outer array. The row arrays inside are still shared with every earlier snapshot.

options.text: Only X's move, because each saved board is one move behind
options.why: Every snapshot points at the same three row arrays, so all of them show every move made so far.

options.text: Both moves, because all snapshots share the same row arrays
options.why: `next[r][c] = ...` writes into a row that `history[0]` also references, so the "start" board is changed too.

options.text: It throws, because writing `next[r][c]` modifies a frozen state array
options.why: React does not freeze state, so the write succeeds silently. That is why the bug is easy to miss.

explanation: Spread is a shallow copy. For nested state, copy every level on the path you change: `board.map((row, i) => i === r ? row.map((v, j) => j === c ? player : v) : row)`, or use a flat array of n * n cells (index `r * n + c`) as the React tutorial does. Shared inner arrays break time travel, `memo` on rows, and any comparison by reference.
reference: react.dev: Updating Arrays in State (Updating objects inside arrays)

options.text: `if (r === c) diag += v; if (r + c === n) anti += v;`
options.why: Off by one: anti-diagonal cells such as (0, n - 1) have `r + c === n - 1`, so the anti-diagonal is never counted correctly.

options.text: `if (r === c) diag += v; else if (r + c === n - 1) anti += v;`
options.why: On an odd board the centre cell lies on both diagonals. The `else` skips the anti-diagonal for it, so that win is missed.

options.text: `if (r === c) diag += v; if (r + c === n - 1) anti += v;`
options.why: Main-diagonal cells have `r === c`, anti-diagonal cells have `r + c === n - 1`, and a cell can be on both.

options.text: `diag += v; anti += v;`
options.why: This counts every move toward both diagonals, so a player "wins" a diagonal without owning it.

explanation: Keeping a counter per row, per column and per diagonal turns the win check into O(1) per move and O(n) memory. Signed values (+1 / -1) let one counter serve both players: a total of ±n means one player owns the whole line, while mixed lines can never reach it. Interviewers use the N x N follow-up to see whether you move beyond a hard-coded list of eight winning lines.
